meta.scope: first 18 entries of rewrite-t27c.json changed[], graded against current content/pilot/existentialism.json and cited corpus sections
meta.quote_check: all 64 cited quotes in these items found verbatim in their cited section (script check); 10 citations are section-only (no quote)

claims.claim: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'certainly not a reference to a coherent system or philosophical school' ... 'one can nonetheless distill a set of overlapping ideas that bind the movement together'

claims.claim: It starts from life as a person lives it (first-person, engaged)
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'existentialism generally begins in medias res, amidst our own situated, first-person experience'

claims.claim: ...not from the detached, objective standpoint that much earlier philosophy preferred
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'Against a philosophical tradition that privileges the standpoint of theoretical detachment and objectivity'; §2: 'From Plato onward, Western philosophy has generally prioritized a methodology grounded in a perspective of rational detachment and objectivity'

claims.claim: We make ourselves through our choices
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'burdened with the task of creating ourselves through our choices and actions'

claims.claim: We are responsible for who we become
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'we are free and responsible for who we are and what we do'

claims.claim: Its ideas began to come together in the nineteenth century
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §1: 'it was not until the nineteenth century that the ideas began to coalesce into a bona fide intellectual movement'

claims.claim: ...with Kierkegaard and Nietzsche
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'laid much earlier in the nineteenth century by pioneers like Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard was from Denmark
claims.evidence: sep-kierkegaard §1: 'He spent most of his life in and around the Danish capital' (same section: 'born ... in Copenhagen on 5 May 1813')

claims.claim: Nietzsche was a German philosopher
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche intro: 'was a German philosopher and cultural critic'

claims.claim: The movement took off in mid-twentieth-century France
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France'

claims.claim: Gabriel Marcel first used the word 'existentialism' in 1943 (so the name took off in France)
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'The word, first introduced by Marcel in 1943'; Marcel listed among French 'compatriots'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir were French
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'the most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir were philosophers and novelists
claims.evidence: sep-sartre intro: 'He also wrote highly influential works of literature'; sep-beauvoir intro: 'was a philosopher, novelist'; sep-existentialism intro: 'the plays, short stories, and novels by French luminaries like Sartre, Beauvoir, and Camus'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir made it famous
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'the most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir'

claims.claim: Only Sartre and Beauvoir called themselves existentialists
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'the major contributors ... of these, only Sartre and Beauvoir explicitly self-identified as “existentialists.”' The source limits this to the major contributors; the same intro calls Norman Mailer 'the self-proclaimed “American existentialist”', so the unqualified 'only' is overstated

claims.claim: Camus was a French novelist
claims.evidence: sep-camus intro: 'novelist and author of short stories'; sep-existentialism intro: 'compatriots such as Albert Camus'

claims.claim: Heidegger was a German philosopher
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'twentieth-century German philosophers like Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger'

claims.claim: Camus rejected the label
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §f: '“Non, je ne suis pas existentialist” is the title of a famous interview'; sep-camus §1: 'Camus denied being an existentialist'

claims.claim: Heidegger rejected the label
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §c: 'There he repudiates any possible connection of his philosophy with the existentialism of Sartre' ... 'given Heidegger’s own repudiation of existentialism'

claims.claim: The encyclopedias still place Camus and Heidegger in the tradition
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §c: 'Heidegger can be classified as an existentialist thinker despite all his differences from Sartre'; sep-camus §1: 'This essay belongs squarely in the philosophical tradition of existentialism'

claims.claim: Existentialists can be religious or not
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'one finds secular and religious existentialists'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard was a religious existentialist, a Christian
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'As a religious existentialist, Kierkegaard contends that this is what is required to enter the sphere of faith and become a Christian'

claims.claim: Nietzsche and Sartre are non-religious existentialists
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §b: 'the existence of a transcendent deity is not relevant to (or is positively detrimental to) such decisions (a view broadly shared by Nietzsche and Sartre)'

items.fix: Of the major figures, only Sartre and Beauvoir called themselves existentialists.

claims.claim: Sartre called existence precedes essence 'the first principle of existentialism'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'This is, according to Sartre, “the first principle of existentialism”'

claims.claim: 'Essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are; we are not born with one
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'there is no pre-given or essential nature that determines us'; intro: 'not as a substance or thing with some pre-given nature (or “essence”)'

claims.claim: A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices as life unfolds
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'man exists, turns up, appears on the scene, and, only afterwards, defines himself' ... 'through the situated choices we make as our lives unfold'

claims.claim: Hard facts still limit us, such as our body and the time and place we live in
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'facts about our situation that limit and constrain us ... our embodiment and spatiality ... and the socio-historical context we find ourselves in'

claims.claim: We can question those facts, give them meaning and decide what to do with them
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'surpass our facticity by calling it into question, interpreting it in different ways, and making decisions about how to deal with it'

claims.claim: A strong craving does not force me to act on it
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §3: 'If I am compelled by a strong desire for sex, alcohol, or cigarettes, for instance, I do not out of necessity have to act on these desires'

claims.claim: This makes us free, and responsible for what we make of ourselves
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4: 'the human being has free will, is able to make decisions, and can be held responsible for their actions'

claims.claim: Sartre's coward is not that way because of childhood or genes
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4: 'the coward ... is not the way he is because of an unstable childhood or a particular genetic makeup'

claims.claim: He 'makes himself a coward' by his decisions
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4: 'The coward “makes himself a coward” by means of his decisions'

claims.claim: Realising this brings anxiety
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4: 'the awareness is often accompanied by anxiety because we realize that we alone are responsible'; §4.1: 'anxiety discloses this predicament to me' (§4 says 'often'; acceptable)

claims.claim: Kierkegaard called anxiety 'the dizziness of freedom'
claims.evidence: sep-kierkegaard §2: 'anxiety is the dizziness of freedom' (the source attributes the line to the pseudonym Haufniensis in The Concept of Anxiety; standard to credit Kierkegaard)

claims.claim: Existentialists ask us to face this feeling, not run from it
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.1: 'we should not close our eyes or flee from these experiences ... the existentialist asks us to turn toward and face it'

claims.claim: It can shake us out of our comfortable routines
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.1: 'uncanny affects that have the power to shake us out of our complacency'

claims.claim: You alone answer for your choices
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4: 'we realize that we alone are responsible for our choices'; §4.1: 'I alone am answerable to whatever options I choose'

claims.claim: That can feel dizzying
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §4.1: 'I face a dizzying array of options'; sep-kierkegaard §2: 'anxiety is the dizziness of freedom'

claims.claim: Being authentic means being true to yourself
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'prevents us from being authentic or true to ourselves'

claims.claim: Existentialists criticise our habit of living by the rules and expectations of those around us
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'critical of our ingrained tendency to conform to the norms and expectations of the public world'

claims.claim: Heidegger's name for this crowd was 'the They'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §1: '“the They” (Heidegger)'; §5: 'doing what “they” do'

claims.claim: We enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: '“We take pleasure and enjoy ourselves as they take pleasure. We read, see, and judge about literature and art as they see and judge”'

claims.claim: It feels like living well
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: 'Living this way can be comforting, creating the illusion that we are living well'

claims.claim: It hides our freedom from us
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: 'unwilling or unable to face up to the freedom and contingency of our condition'; 'it covers over the anxiety of own freedom and finitude'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: 'Sartre and Beauvoir refer to inauthenticity in terms of “bad faith”'; conformism is 'a manifestation of inauthenticity or self-deception'

claims.claim: Bad faith comes in two forms
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: 'where we either deny or over-identify with one of the two aspects of human existence, either facticity or transcendence'

claims.claim: Form 1: treating yourself as a fixed thing, 'I am what I am', nothing can change me
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: 'as if I were a fully realized object or thing ... that “I am what I am,” and there is nothing that can change me'

claims.claim: Form 2: pretending you have no limits, as if past and situation did not constrain choices
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5: 'when I over-identify with freedom and deny my past conduct and the fact that my choices are limited and constrained by my situation'

claims.claim: What authenticity looks like varies by thinker
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2-5.5 give separate accounts per thinker

claims.claim: Kierkegaard: a passionate commitment that unifies a scattered life
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'a passionate, “personality defining” ... decision or commitment that binds together and unifies the fragmented and disjointed moments of our life'

claims.claim: Nietzsche: creating your own values
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.3: 'the self-directed power to create their own meanings and values'

claims.claim: Nietzsche: saying yes to your whole life
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.3: 'The Overman is a “yes-sayer” who affirms every aspect of his life'

claims.claim: Heidegger: pulling your life together around what matters to you
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.4: 'I “pull [myself] together,” giving life a sense of cohesion and focus'; 'seize hold of the publicly interpreted meanings that matter to me'

claims.claim: Heidegger: staying ready to let it go if circumstances change
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.4: 'I must also be willing to let go or give up on them depending on the circumstances of my life'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir: facing your unsettled situation clearly
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: 'a clear-eyed awareness and acceptance of the instability and ambiguity of the human condition'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir: taking responsibility for what you do
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: 'a willingness to act in the face of this ambiguity and to take responsibility'; 'It is to be concerned with what I do'

claims.claim: The old religious answers faded
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §1: 'the traditional religious framework that gave pre-modern life a sense of moral orientation and cohesion was beginning to collapse'

claims.claim: Three thinkers (Nietzsche, Camus, Beauvoir) asked how life can still mean something
claims.evidence: sep-camus §3.4: 'This is how a life without ultimate meaning can be made worth living'; sep-existentialism §5.3 (Nietzsche creating meanings), §5.5 (Beauvoir on meaning)

claims.claim: Nineteenth-century Europe grew less religious and more scientific
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'late nineteenth century Europe as the pre-modern religious worldview was replaced with one that was increasingly secular and scientific'

claims.claim: The old picture that gave life moral direction began to collapse
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §1: 'the traditional religious framework that gave pre-modern life a sense of moral orientation and cohesion was beginning to collapse'

claims.claim: Nihilism: the shocking sense that our existence has no overall reason or purpose
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §1: 'the shocking recognition that there is no overarching reason, order, or purpose to our existence'

claims.claim: Nietzsche summed up the crisis as 'God is dead'
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche §2: 'he launches the famous, aggressive and paradoxical pronouncement that “God is dead”'; sep-existentialism §5.3: 'against the backdrop of God’s death'

claims.claim: 'God is dead' does not mean God literally died
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche §2: 'The idea is not so much that atheism is true—in GS 125, he depicts this pronouncement arriving as fresh news to a group of atheists—but instead that...'. The cited quote denies the atheism reading (a claim that there is no God), not a 'literal death' reading; the gloss swaps the contrast the source draws

claims.claim: Belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche §2: 'because “the belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable”'

claims.claim: So the morality built on it was set to collapse
claims.evidence: sep-nietzsche §2: 'everything that was “built upon this faith ...”, including “the whole of our European morality”, is destined for “collapse”'

claims.claim: Nietzsche's answer: create your own values
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.3: 'create their own meanings and values against the backdrop of God’s death'

claims.claim: Camus called our situation 'the absurd'
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §f: 'Camus is known for his conception of the absurd'

claims.claim: The absurd is the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'
claims.evidence: sep-camus §3.3: 'an inevitable divorce between human consciousness, with its “wild longing for clarity” (MS, 21) and the “unreasonable silence of the world”'; iep §f: 'the space which opens up between ... man’s need for intelligibility and ... ‘the unreasonable silence of the world’'

claims.claim: Camus asked whether life is still worth living or suicide is the answer
claims.evidence: sep-camus §3.1: '“There is only one really serious philosophical problem ... and that is suicide. Deciding whether or not life is worth living ...”'

claims.claim: He said it is worth living
claims.evidence: sep-camus §3.4: 'This is how a life without ultimate meaning can be made worth living'

claims.claim: Reject suicide and false hope
claims.evidence: iep-camus §c: 'In the end, Camus rejects suicide: the Absurd must not be evaded either by religion ... or by annihilation'; sep-camus §3.4: 'avoiding false solutions such as religion'

claims.claim: Live fully aware
claims.evidence: sep-camus §3.4: 'Full consciousness ... carrying on with vitality and intensity'

claims.claim: Beauvoir said existence is not absurd, since that would mean it can never be given a meaning
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: '“The notion of ambiguity must not be confused with that of absurdity. To declare that existence is absurd is to deny that it can ever be given a meaning”'

claims.claim: It is 'ambiguous': 'its meaning is never fixed'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: 'to say that it is ambiguous is to assert that its meaning is never fixed'

claims.claim: So we keep making it
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.5: 'My projects have meaning and value because I chose these projects, but the meaning is contingent; it is never enduring or stable'

items.fix: Nietzsche summed up the crisis as 'God is dead': not mainly a claim that there is no God, but that belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so the morality built on it was set to collapse.

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6.1: 'Sartre and Beauvoir argue ... I understand or see myself in the way that I do through “the look” (le regard) of the Other'

claims.claim: Their gaze can turn us into objects
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6.1: 'the look has the power to strip away my freedom and turn me into an object'

claims.claim: Sartre's example: peeping through a keyhole, lost in the scene
claims.evidence: sep-sartre §4.3: 'we are asked to imagine that we are peeping through a keyhole, pre-reflectively immersed and absorbed in the scene'

claims.claim: Hearing footsteps, you feel shame as you see yourself as an object in someone else's eyes
claims.evidence: sep-sartre §4.3: 'Suddenly, though, we hear footsteps, and we have an involuntary apprehension of ourselves as an object in the eyes of another; a “pre-moral” experience of shame'

claims.claim: Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in the line that hell is other people
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6.1: 'This struggle for self-assertion leads to Sartre’s famous claim in his play Huis Clos (No Exit) that “Hell is—other people”'

claims.claim: Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other's freedom instead of possessing them
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6.1: '“authentic love” ... a relationship where we acknowledge and nurture the other’s freedom ... resisting ... to see the Other as an object or thing to be manipulated and possessed'

claims.claim: If I see freedom as my core, I must see it as others' core and help them realise it
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6: 'When I acknowledge that freedom is my essence, I must also acknowledge that it is the essence of others and work, to the best of my ability, to help them realize it'

claims.claim: Sartre: in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §6: 'And in wanting freedom we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard prized 'a truth which is true for me'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §2.1: 'it discloses “a truth which is true for me”'

claims.claim: That truth is lived and felt rather than proved
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §2.1: 'subjective truth cannot be reasoned about or explained logically'; 'It is an ineffable truth that is felt rather than known'

claims.claim: In Fear and Trembling he retells the Bible story of Abraham
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §a: 'Fear and Trembling retells the story of the attempted sacrifice of Isaac by his father Abraham'; sep-existentialism §5.2: 'draws on the biblical figure of Abraham'

claims.claim: God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §a: 'God tells Abraham that in order to prove his faith he has to sacrifice his only son'

claims.claim: As a father, Abraham has a moral duty to protect his son
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'As a father, Abraham has a moral duty to love and protect his son'

claims.claim: Abraham obeys
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §a: 'Abraham obeys'

claims.claim: At the last moment God intervenes and saves Isaac
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §a: 'but at the last moment God intervenes and saves Isaac'

claims.claim: Faith can put a personal truth above ordinary morality
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'he is confronted with a personal truth that is higher than the universal'; 'the subjective truth of the individual is higher than the universal truths of morality'

claims.claim: It is a truth reason cannot make sense of
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'a willingness to commit to a truth that is fundamentally irrational and absurd. How, for example, can one make rational sense of God’s command'

claims.claim: Committing to it is a 'leap'
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'Abraham becomes a “knight of faith” by “leaping” (springer) into a paradox'

claims.claim: The leap is a choice no argument can justify
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'a truth that is fundamentally irrational and absurd'; 'he “cannot make himself understood to anyone”'

claims.claim: It cuts you off from what everyone else thinks right
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism §5.2: 'it cuts us off from the comforting truths of the public and its blanket conceptions of right and wrong'

claims.claim: One encyclopedia names the worry: what if someone excused violence as a command of God?
claims.evidence: iep-existentialism §a: 'Is not such a subjectivist model of truth and religion plainly dangerous? What if someone was to support his acts of violence as a command of God?'

claims.claim: In mid-twentieth-century France, the movement's backdrop was WWII, the Nazi death camps and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
claims.evidence: sep-existentialism intro: 'exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France ... emerged against the backdrop of the Second World War, the Nazi death camps, and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki' (source hedges 'often viewed as'; scoped to France mid-century, so fair)

claims.claim: The works that follow are in chronological order
claims.evidence: works list years ascend: 1843, 1882, 1927, 1942, 1943, 1945, 1949 (each year sourced on its own works item; works items not graded in this batch)
